questions.q: Why isn't successfully deploying a control the same as confirming it reduced risk?
options: Risk reduction is guaranteed once a control passes pilot testing
A control can be live, enforced, and stable while doing nothing measurable to reduce the risk it was built for
Deployment and risk reduction are always the same claim
Every control that deploys successfully automatically reduces risk
questions.explain: Shipping and working are two different claims; only measurement tells you whether the control's real-world effect matched its intent.

questions.q: Why does this lesson insist on recording a baseline before a control ships?
options: Baselines are only needed for Conditional Access policies, not other controls
Secure Score automatically creates a baseline with no manual recording needed
You can't tell if anything changed if you never recorded what conditions looked like before the change
A baseline replaces the need to ever measure results after deployment
questions.explain: A baseline that only exists in someone's memory isn't a real baseline — it needs to be recorded with a date before the change ships.

questions.q: In the lesson's example, what did the before/after risky sign-in alert numbers (47 vs. 9) demonstrate?
options: That Secure Score had increased, with no other metric involved
A real, measured 81% drop in risky sign-in alerts over the same window, compared against a recorded baseline
That the Conditional Access policy had been disabled
That the numbers were anecdotal and could not be trusted
questions.explain: Measuring the same metric over the same window against a real baseline is what turns the numbers into evidence rather than an anecdote.

questions.q: What does Microsoft Secure Score actually measure, according to this lesson?
options: Only the strength of individual users' passwords
The exact number of security incidents prevented by a given control
Whether specific recommended controls are configured, which is a signal but not direct proof of real-world risk reduction
Nothing related to security configuration at all
questions.explain: Secure Score confirms a control is configured as expected, but incident and alert counts are what show whether real risk actually went down.

questions.q: Why is a single good-looking week of metrics right after rollout, with no defined baseline, not real evidence?
options: A single week of data is always statistically significant on its own
Secure Score alone always resolves this problem automatically
Without a recorded "before" baseline and a comparable measurement window, there's nothing valid to compare it against
Metrics gathered after rollout are never useful for any purpose
questions.explain: The lesson calls this an anecdote rather than evidence, because evidence requires a real baseline and a matching measurement window.
